workload: Parallel decompression of gzip-compressed ASCII text files (FASTQ in the paper; 2.7 GB and 24 GB compressed files in the README), speed measured in compressed input bytes per second
claimed_speedup: README, dual Xeon X5675: gunzip 55 MB/s vs pugz 147 MB/s with 1 thread and 251 MB/s full decompression with 24 threads (1052 MB/s when only counting lines); i7-4770: gunzip 63 MB/s vs pugz 172 MB/s (1 thread) and 376 MB/s (8 threads). Paper Table II (32 threads, FASTQ files preloaded in memory): gunzip 37 MB/s, libdeflate 118 MB/s, pugz 611 MB/s, stated as 16.5x faster than gunzip and 5.2x faster than libdeflate
compiler_and_flags: README: make asserts=0 for maximal performance; compiler and version not stated
hardware: README: dual Xeon X5675 (2x 6C/12T, 32 GB) and i7-4770 (4C/8T, 16 GB); paper: 2x12-core 2.3 GHz Xeon E5-2670 v3, 512 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 124 stars; paper by Kerbiriou and Chikhi (copy in repo at paper/paper.pdf)
tradeoffs: Only ASCII text files with bytes in ['\t','~'] work (no binary, no .tar.gz); no CRC32 check (README says adding it would cost about 33%); no multi-member gzip support; standalone program, not a library; output synchronization limits the in-order speedup; needs many cores to win (1 thread: 147 vs 55 MB/s likely reflects its libdeflate-derived inflate code, per the README).
caveats: Prototype, may crash or give undefined behavior with asserts off. Paper speeds write output unsynchronized to /dev/null, which the paper says mimics an order-insensitive FASTQ parser; the README full-decompression column keeps ordered output. The paper PDF text I read does not name its publication venue, so no peer-review credit is claimed; compiler version and flags are not stated. The newer project rapidgzip (already catalogued) covers the general case.

Lexicographic exactMatchSearch: JA1 48.9 vs 33.1 ns/key. Dictionary size halved (JA1 7,023 KB vs 3,336 KB; EN2 513,873 KB vs 240,634 KB). Build time lower (JA1 828 vs 368 ns/key). Author attributes the speedup to better cache use from the smaller dictionary.

Not a true succinct structure: it is a compact double-array trie (32-bit units, DAWG-merged), so it is far larger than LOUDS or MARISA tries (marisa-trie README lists 376,613,888 bytes for darts-clone against 50,753,560 for marisa-trie on 9.8M Wikipedia titles). Results are mixed: on the postal-code set (DIG) Darts-clone is slower for exactMatchSearch (24.2 vs 18.8 ns/key lexicographic), and traverse() is slower on most word lists (for example JA2 144.6 vs 119.1 ns/key lexicographic). The page itself warns that search time depends heavily on cache sizes, inlining and key distribution. On the large Wikipedia and n-gram sets the random-order gain is smaller (JA2 516.4 vs 620.8 ns/key). Found as a registry hit, but it is a compact trie rather than a rank/select structure, so category fit is loose.
